1:
The verse is a sentence that never finishes, and the commentators spend their strength on where it resumes. Robertson takes the opening phrase as a preposition governing the genitive and pointing back to the argument about God's elective grace, and suggests that Paul actually began the prayer that stands at the end of the chapter, only to be diverted by his own words — the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — into the rich paragraph that follows. Ellicott agrees that the nominative "I, Paul" must be carried on past the whole digression, and puts the one remaining question sharply: does the sentence resume at "I desire that ye faint not," or at "I bow my knees"? He decides for the latter, on two grounds — the emphatic repetition of "for this cause," and the far greater weight and finality of that sentence. Henry, working from the sense rather than the syntax, offers both readings of the opening phrase without choosing between them: either it looks back, so that Paul is a prisoner for having taught that gospel privileges belong to uncircumcised Gentiles, or it looks forward, so that because they are no longer strangers he prays they may live as men so favoured — and on that reading the thread is picked up again after the digression.

Barnes presses a translator's point that follows from the same observation. Since no verb is expressed, the rendering ought to be "For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner," which is how Tindale gave it — I, Paul, the servant of Jesus, am in bonds — and how Locke, Rosenmüller, Doddridge, Whitby and Koppe understood it; the abruptness of the common version then disappears. He is emphatic that this was no captivity for crime, for debt, or in war, but bondage in the Redeemer's service, and takes the words as proof that Paul was in bonds at Rome when he wrote. Clarke and Gill supply the history behind that. Because Paul maintained that the Gentiles were admitted to every privilege of the covenant without submitting to circumcision, the Jews persecuted him to bonds and conspired his death; he was held first at Caesarea, appealed to the emperor, and was sent on to Rome. Gill draws the pastoral consequence: since the imprisonment was for no capital crime, Paul was not ashamed of his chains but gloried in them, a prison having often been the portion of the best of men; and because he suffered on the Ephesians' own account, the very fact of his suffering confirmed the doctrine he had delivered to them. Wesley states the benefit plainly — a prisoner for the Gentiles, for their advantage, and for asserting their right to these blessings.

Calvin sees the chains as contested ground. What ought to have confirmed the apostleship was turned by Paul's adversaries to the opposite use, so he answers by speaking of his prison in lofty terms — before the world such talk would be foolish boasting, but among godly persons it is dignified and faithful. The glory of Christ does not merely overcome the ignominy of a chain; it converts what was a reproach into the highest honour, so that the crowns and sceptres of kings are less honourable than the bonds of a prisoner of Jesus Christ. Ellicott reaches the same end by another road, calling the phrase a striking instance of the spiritual alchemy of faith that turns all things to good, and reading the captivity as ordained by the Lord's own will, which makes Paul an ambassador in chains whose imprisonment shows that the word of God is not bound. Henry puts it most simply: Christ's servants, if they come to be prisoners, are his prisoners, and he thinks never the worse of them for the character the world gives them.
2:
The conditional particle is not a real condition. Barnes, citing Robinson, glosses it as spoken of what is taken for granted, and prefers Doddridge's "since I well know you have heard"; Clarke says the compound particle often means since indeed or seeing that and should be so rendered here, the Ephesians having learned it amply while Paul was among them, since he had not shunned to declare the whole counsel of God. Robertson, calling it a first-class condition, notes that the intensive particle gives a delicate touch to it all. On the noun, Gill weighs three senses and settles on the last: not the free love in God's heart toward his people, nor grace wrought inwardly in Paul, but the doctrine of grace itself, the gospel whose subject matter is God's free favour and which is also the means of conveying that favour into the heart. Clarke allows both office and knowledge: either the apostolic commission and gifts granted for preaching among the Gentiles, or the understanding God gave Paul of the plan he had formed for their conversion. Wesley keeps it to the commission, and adds that the Ephesians had heard of it from Paul's own mouth.

Clarke opens the next clause with a textual note. For "he made known" a long list of witnesses reads "was made known" — the uncials he lists, with the Syriac, Coptic, Slavonic, Vulgate and Itala, and Clement, Cyril, Chrysostom and Theodoret — and judges it doubtless the true reading; the point being that the doctrine was no opinion of Paul's own, nor gathered from the ancient prophets, but came by immediate revelation. Calvin uses the same word to draw a line. The novelty of the case had few supporters, and calling it a mystery removes the prejudice that the general displeasure was fitted to excite; but it also separates Paul from the fanatics who ascribe their own idle dreams to God and the Holy Spirit. False apostles boast of revelations, and the boast is false; Paul was persuaded his was true, could prove it to others, and speaks of it as a thing beyond doubt. Barnes guards the term from a different misuse: the mystery of Christ has nothing to do with anything mysterious in Christ's person, in the union of the two natures, or in the atonement, but means the hitherto concealed doctrine that the Gentiles were to be received to the same privileges as the Jews. Wesley says the same in a line — salvation by Christ alone, and that to Jews and Gentiles both.

"As I wrote afore in few words" divides them. Robertson lays out three possibilities — an epistolary aorist for this letter, a previous and lost letter, or the preceding discussion of the Gentiles — and calls the last possible and also probable; he adds that the phrase rendered "in few words" means briefly, not shortly before. Barnes reports that Bloomfield, Doddridge, Rosenmüller, Erasmus, Grotius and Locke all take it of the two foregoing chapters, and inclines that way himself, since the words "whereby, when ye read" seem to point at what he had just written. Calvin prefers the lost letter, which he calls the general opinion, and turns the loss into an argument about the canon: given Paul's watchfulness, zeal and readiness to help, it is highly probable he wrote many letters, public and private, and those the Lord judged necessary for his church his providence has preserved. There is therefore no room for the sneers of the ungodly, as though the Scriptures had been mutilated; what remains is enough, and the smallness of the number is not accident but a body adjusted by the wonderful counsel of God. Gill and Robertson agree on the reading Paul expects: the letter will be read in public, and by that bare reading his grasp of the mystery may be judged.
5:
Calvin faces the obvious objection head on. If the prophets everywhere declared that people would come from every nation to worship God, that an altar should be raised in Assyria and in Egypt, that the Messiah should hold dominion from east to west — how could this be hidden, and why is every one pronounced ignorant? Shall we say the prophets uttered sounds without meaning? His answer is that Paul does not mean there had been no knowledge at all. Some Jews had always acknowledged that at the Messiah's advent grace would be proclaimed throughout the world; but the prophets, speaking with the certainty of revelation, left the time and manner undetermined. The apostles are his proof: they had the predictions, had heard from their Master of other sheep not of this fold, and had received the charge to preach to every creature — and still recoiled from the calling of the Gentiles as absolutely monstrous, because the manner of it was unknown and the ceremonies were a veil over their face. Gill measures the same reticence: hints to Adam after the fall, the gospel preached to Abraham, more given through Isaiah, but the whole lying hid in types, shadows and short obscure hints. Clarke sharpens what was genuinely new. That the Gentiles would be called the prophets had made exceedingly clear; that they should be saved without taking on the yoke of the Mosaic law, and that the Jews themselves should be freed from it, had not been made known at all.

Ellicott reads the two designations as a deliberate pair. "The sons of men" is an Old Testament phrase, frequent in the poetical books and the standing form of address to Ezekiel; it should not be narrowed to Israel or to the prophets, since by nature it covers all mankind, but it carries a suggestion of the old dispensation set against the new. Against it stands the epithet "holy," applied to the apostles by one of their own number — thought strange, he grants, though natural enough in the impersonal style of an encyclical. The word marks not personal character but official call and privilege. Wesley presses the Ezekiel echo further: not made known to any man, not even to the prophet so often styled son of man, and the prophets here named are those of the New Testament. Barnes agrees on the identification and draws a conclusion about the office: those who prophesied in the Christian church were genuinely inspired, but there is no evidence the order was meant to be permanent — it was needed while the church was being settled and the written revelation was incomplete, and when the volume of revelation was finished its function ceased. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse for another purpose, citing it among his proofs that the Holy Spirit subsists, lives, speaks and foretells.

Robertson counts the vocabulary. Paul is fond of compounds with the preposition meaning "together," and uses three of them in a row: fellow-heirs, late and rare; fellow-members of the body, found first here and nowhere else outside later ecclesiastical writers; and fellow-partakers, another late and rare word that appears in one papyrus for the joint possessor of a house. On the ministry that follows, Calvin is anxious that nothing be claimed as desert. Paul calls it a gift and an exhibition of divine power — inquire not what I deserved, nor what I formerly was, for it is the Lord's prerogative to exalt them of low degree and to produce something great out of nothing. Barnes takes the phrase about effectual working in a direction Locke did not. Locke referred the energy of God's power to the conversion of the Gentiles under Paul's ministry; Barnes refers it rather to the conversion of Paul himself, since his opposition to the gospel was such that nothing less than that energy could have overcome it.
8:
The self-description is a manufactured word, and the grammarians linger over it. Clarke explains the manufacture: to lay himself as low as possible while still counting among divinely commissioned men, Paul builds a comparative not, as regular procedure would require, on the positive, but on the superlative — from the word for little he takes the superlative meaning least and forms from that a comparative meaning less than the least. It would be vain, Clarke adds, to attempt a better rendering than the one our version gives. Barnes calls it one of a class of expressions peculiar to Paul, where ordinary language will not carry the idea and a word is therefore coined to carry it more emphatically; it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, though Bloomfield and Rosenmüller supply parallels from later Greek writers, and it means incomparably the least, or not worthy to be reckoned among the saints at all. Robertson finds the formation less startling: the same thing was already done in older Greek, and he compares a double comparative elsewhere in the New Testament. He enters one caution the others do not. This was not mock humility, for on occasion Paul stood up firmly for his rights as an apostle.

Chrysostom makes the phrase the lesson of the day. Those who go to the physician's must not merely go, but learn how to treat themselves; so those who come here must learn the surpassing lowliness of Paul. He weighs the words precisely. Paul does not say less than the apostles — that expression, "I am not meet to be called an apostle," is the weaker of the two — but less than the least of all the saints; and to say this after so many great and good deeds, and at that time of life, is surpassing moderation. Calvin insists the confession is sincere. Most men make professions of feigned humility while their minds are swelled with pride, calling themselves inferior to everyone while wanting the highest esteem; Paul is not of that number, and elsewhere speaks of himself in still more degrading language. But he adds the necessary qualification: when Paul calls himself the meanest of all, he is confining his attention to what he was in himself, apart from the grace of God. Gill turns it into a rule — the greatest saints are generally the most humble, having the largest discoveries of grace and the keenest sense of their own vileness, and boughs laden with fruit hang lowest. Wesley simply calls it the noblest strain of eloquence.

"Unsearchable" is a footprint word, and both Ellicott and Clarke work the metaphor. It means, properly, that the tracks can be followed but not traced home to their source or issue, so that one gains evidence of a living power without knowing whence it comes or whither it goes; applied here to the wealth of Christ, it marks a wealth of truth we can see in part but cannot measure and a wealth of grace we can enjoy but cannot exhaust. Clarke refers the footsteps to God's own — the plans formed, the dispensations published, the innumerable providences combined to bring the design of salvation to effect — and observes that the abundance was too great to be comprehended even by the apostle's capacious mind. Hence, he says, Paul's letters taken in chronological order show his views brightening and his discoveries growing more distinct as he advances; had he lived and written to the present day he would not have exhausted the subject. Henry adds the pastoral edge that the others leave implicit. Many are not enriched with these riches, yet it is a great favour to have them preached among us and to have the offer made; and if we are not enriched with them, the fault is our own.
9:
Three of the commentators agree that the received text is wrong here. Where our version reads "fellowship," Clarke reports the reading "dispensation" in the great uncials and more than fifty other manuscripts, in the Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Slavonian, Vulgate and Itala, and in the chief of the Greek fathers, and holds that the common text has very little authority behind it; Griesbach received the better reading into his text. Barnes lists Griesbach, Tittman, Rosenmüller and Koppe as adopting it and notes how easily a transcriber could make the slip, though he adds that the point is not very material to the sense. Ellicott says manuscript authority and internal evidence point the same way, and takes the phrase of the order God himself has ordained for manifesting the truth to men and angels rather than of the commission given to Paul. Barnes is unwilling to let the older reading go without extracting its value. Following Whately, he sets it against the pagan mysteries, where initiated and uninitiated were divided and the Eleusinian rites had greater and lesser doctrines: in contrast, Christianity conceals nothing from any part of its adherents, has no reserved doctrines, and entrusts no truths to a sacred priesthood alone.

"To make all men see" is, in the Greek, to illuminate, and Ellicott finds our rendering at once too strong and too weak. Too weak, because the verb is the one used of the eyes of the heart being enlightened; too strong, because while we can enlighten, it is our daily sorrow that we cannot make men see — even the Lord wept over Jerusalem, whose wilful blindness hid his light from their eyes. Opening the eyes and turning men from darkness to light is attributed in general terms to God's servants, since it naturally follows their ministry, but it is properly the work of the Spirit. Robertson makes the same point in a sentence: the verb is to turn the light on, and only one whose own heart-eyes are enlightened can turn it for others. Gill states the division of labour flatly — ministers enlighten instrumentally, God alone efficiently — and takes "all men" as some of all sorts, not every individual in the world. Calvin hears in the metaphor a claim that in Paul's apostleship the grace of God shines with the brightness of noon-day, and turns it against the impatience of readers who resent being kept in ignorance of anything: who will question God's right to keep his own purposes concealed until he pleases to communicate them?

The closing words "by Jesus Christ" fare worse still. Clarke finds them absent from the leading uncials, from the Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Vulgate and Itala and several fathers; Griesbach threw them out, and Professor White pronounced them indisputably to be deleted. Clarke draws the doctrinal moral at once: no inferiority of Christ can be argued from a clause whose spuriousness is so strongly attested. Barnes reaches the same verdict by another route, citing Mill's suggestion that a transcriber inserted the phrase from the parallel in Colossians, and observing that nothing is lost either way, since the doctrine is abundantly taught elsewhere. Ellicott agrees the words crept in from a gloss, and holds that the emphasis lies rather on the bare description of God as the creator of all things, material and spiritual, which fixes the gospel in the primeval purpose of the divine mind. Calvin, reading the clause as genuine, hesitates between the first creation and the spiritual renewal, and inclines to the latter — while allowing the argument that if the Father created all things by Christ as God, it is no wonder that by Christ as Mediator the Gentiles are brought back into one body. Wesley compresses the whole into a phrase: God created all things to make way for the free exercise of his love.
10:
Who the principalities and powers are is disputed. Clarke lays out three candidates — evil angels, good angels, or the Jewish rulers and rabbins converted to Christianity — and reports Macknight's judgement that the orders of angels are meant, whose knowledge of God's dispensations must be as gradual as those dispensations themselves. Gill decides briskly for the good angels, ruling out civil magistrates and, still more, evil ones. Calvin knows the objection that ignorance cannot be found in beings permitted to behold the brightness of God's countenance, and that some therefore refer the words to devils; but he thinks this said without due reflection: what would be remarkable in the news that devils had been informed of something? The church, he concludes, is a mirror in which angels behold a wisdom new to them, and it is by seeing the work, not by learning at the lips of men, that they make progress — so the inference that angels attend our assemblies and advance in knowledge alongside us is a groundless speculation. Ellicott presses the thought outward instead: the angels are our fellow-learners in the school of Christ, and this world, itself a speck in the universe, may be a lesson to other spheres of being far beyond our conception.

The adjective translated "manifold" means many-coloured, and everyone reaches for a picture. Robertson notes it is an old and rare word, found nowhere else in the New Testament. Barnes takes it as greatly diversified rather than merely great, a well-ordered variety of dispensations — wisdom in forming the plan, in selecting the Redeemer, in the incarnation, in the atonement, in renewing the heart — and likens it to a panorama passing before the mind, or to the changing beauty of clouds at evening with the sun reflected on them, each aspect differing and all raising the mind to God. Ellicott, calling it properly many-coloured or wrought in many details, observes that it is used of God's wisdom here and nowhere else, and finds it displayed in the infinite variety of the church's teaching and life — manifold, yet one, since it embodies a single life. Calvin puts the accent on our narrowness: men try this wisdom by a false standard, confining their view to one department, as the Jews supposed the dispensation under the law the only form it could take. Clarke adds the note of security — plans laid on an infinite scale and accomplished by endless means, which no cunning or malice of men or devils can defeat. Wesley calls the church the theatre of the divine wisdom.

On "the eternal purpose" Barnes and Clarke collide directly. Clarke renders the phrase as a purpose concerning the periods, arguing that the word for age is often applied to whole systems taken from commencement to termination — God appointing when the Jewish dispensation should begin and end, when the gospel should succeed it, and that the results of both be endless. Barnes names Clarke, with Locke, Chandler and Whitby, as taking it of an arrangement of the ages, and rejects the reading as wholly at variance with the settled use of the word, suspecting that its real object is to avoid the doctrine that God has a plan at all. He will not have that avoided: who could respect an intelligent Being who had no purpose and did everything by caprice and hazard? and if God has a plan, it must be eternal, since he has no new schemes. Gill and Calvin close from the same side: no new will can arise in God, and Calvin notes that this is the third time the decree is called eternal and unchangeable, a guard against the suspicion that it had altered. Ellicott adds a grammatical correction — the second verb is not the noun repeated but a distinct word meaning wrought or made, and the sense of working out suits better.
12:
Two nouns govern the verse, and the expositors take them as a pair. Gill reads the access as entrance into the holy of holies, to the throne of grace and to the Father seated upon it, with Christ as the way and union to him as the right; the boldness he analyses into a liberty granted from God's side and a liberty felt on ours — freedom to speak out the mind plainly, and a holy courage free from servile fear, which rests on a heart sprinkled from an evil conscience and a view of God as a God of peace. Wesley supplies two homely pictures for the same pair: access such as petitioners have who are brought before the king by a distinguished favourite, and boldness such as children use with an indulgent father, disclosing all their wants without fear of giving offence. Clarke keeps to the practical inference. It is only in Christ's name that we may pray and only by him that we may come, since none else can give us an introduction; and it is on the ground of such passages as this, he says, that we close all our prayers in the name and for the sake of Jesus Christ our Lord.

Ellicott separates the two more sharply. Boldness, prompted by the charge of proclaiming the mystery, is boldness of thought and utterance before men and angels; access in confidence is the assurance before God that belongs to those who are no longer servants but sons. Each rests on faith, but on a different aspect of it — faith in Christ's teaching and grace for the first, faith in his atonement and gift of new life for the second. Robertson settles the grammar of the phrase in a line: the genitive is objective, so the faith is faith in him. Calvin makes the verse a definition. There are three stages in our progress: we believe the promises of God; relying on them we obtain a trust accompanied by holiness and peace of mind; and last comes the confidence that banishes fear and brings us steadily into God's presence. To separate confidence from faith would be to take heat and light from the sun. He grants that the measure varies, greater in some and smaller in others, but never absent, so that a trembling and doubting conscience is sure evidence of unbelief; and he charges the schoolmen who enjoin men to hesitate with not knowing what it is to call upon God at all.

The verb translated "faint" carries more than weariness. Barnes gives it as turning out a coward, notes Locke's "dismayed," and rejects Koppe's account of the danger — the risk was not that the Ephesians would think the religion false because Paul suffered, but that they would grow disheartened in their attachment to a faith which exposed its friends to such calamities. Calvin cites Chandler for the same military sense, to behave like a coward and through fear desert the post of battle, and cannot restrain his admiration: what a heroic breast, that drew from a prison and from death itself comfort for those who were in no danger. He adds the reason it worked — the faith of a people is powerfully confirmed when a pastor does not hesitate to seal his doctrine by the surrender of his life, so that the churches had good cause to glory in seeing their faith ratified by the best of pledges. Henry notices that Paul seems more anxious lest the believers be discouraged by his tribulations than about what he had himself to bear, and Wesley reduces the clause to five words: the not fainting is your glory.
14:
Where the sentence resumes is asked once more. Henry takes the apostle to be picking up what he began at the first verse, after the long digression that intervened; Barnes reports Bloomfield to that effect but himself prefers a reference to what immediately precedes — that the purposes of these sufferings may be answered in your benefit and glory, I bow my knees. Ellicott, who had earlier weighed the same question, describes what now follows as a prayer addressed with special emphasis to the Father of all: that by the strengthening grace of the Spirit and the indwelling of Christ, accepted in faith and deepened by love, they may first know the mystery already described in all its greatness, and then learn by experience the unsearchable love of Christ dwelling in them, and so be filled up to the fulness of God. Calvin notices why the prayer is reported at all. It testifies Paul's regard for them, but it is also meant to stir them to pray likewise — the seed of the word being scattered in vain unless the Lord makes it fruitful. Gill names the particular request as perseverance, which is the pure gift of God and promised by him, and therefore precisely the thing he must be asked for.

The posture divides them sharply. Clarke turns the clause into a rebuke of his own contemporaries: what can a man think of himself who in addressing God either sits in his seat or stands? He would not sit while speaking to a person of ordinary respectability, and would not be permitted to sit before the king of his own land — is God then to be treated with less respect than a fellow mortal? He musters the examples of Paul, Stephen and Peter kneeling, and finds in the whole prayer a resemblance to Solomon's at the dedication of the temple, Paul now dedicating the Christian church to the same God. Barnes agrees that kneeling is the usual and proper posture and calls it an unhappy thing that the custom has been departed from in the churches. Gill and Calvin decline the argument. A man is not tied to any particular gesture, says Gill; the main thing is the heart, and mere postures are insignificant things with God, though where the mind is affected the body will be moved. Calvin makes the attitude stand for the exercise itself, adding only that this expression of reverence is the one commonly employed where the prayer is a continued one rather than an incidental petition. Robertson doubts Calvin's supposition that Paul knelt as he dictated.

The name of the one addressed is itself disputed. Ellicott holds that the words "of our Lord Jesus Christ" are an interpolation on both external and internal evidence, probably from a gloss meant to indicate — in the true spirit of the letter — that the universal Fatherhood here spoken of is derived from the fatherly relation to him in whom all things are gathered up. Clarke reports the same omission in very ancient and excellent manuscripts and versions, where the clause reads simply that he bows his knees to the Father. Barnes, taking the longer text, uses it to settle a question of practice: prayer is ordinarily to be addressed to the Father, though this does not make it improper to address the Lord Jesus. Calvin draws a different practical conclusion, and aims it at pastors. The Lord alone acts upon us, but he acts by his own instruments; so the Spirit's work of enlightening minds does not render instruction superfluous, as Pelagians and Papists argue, but gives instruction its weight and efficacy. Neither may a minister take it as an excuse for sloth: his business is to labour earnestly in sowing and watering, while asking and expecting the increase from God alone.
15:
"Of whom" has two possible antecedents and the commentators split. Barnes lists Bloomfield, Chandler, Erasmus and Koppe for the Father, and Locke, Doddridge and Calvin for the Lord Jesus, and judges the second the more natural; Wesley takes the first without argument; Gill allows either, since Christ too is called the everlasting Father and is the firstborn among many brethren. Calvin argues the case. The relative may apply equally to Father or to Son, and he objects to Erasmus for restricting it to the Father, since readers ought to have been left a choice; but he thinks referring it to the Father is exposed to a plain difficulty — God formerly passed the Gentiles by and adopted the Jews as his peculiar people, whereas the whole point here is that the distinction is gone. Applied to Christ the statement fits the facts: through his mediation Jews and Gentiles are one family, and may claim kindred even with angels. Barnes adds a Jewish usage from Wetstein that bears on the same phrase — the rabbis called the angels God's upper family and his people on earth his lower family — though he doubts that "in heaven" here means the Jews as distinguished from the Gentiles.

The noun itself invites a famous mistranslation. Ellicott reports the proposal to render it "fatherhood" — from whom all fatherhood derives its name, every lower fatherhood being a shadow of God's — and calls it tempting, yielding a grand sense that agrees with the treatment of earthly relationships later in the letter; but the usage of the word is clearly against it, and it must be rendered every family, that is, every body of rational beings in earth or heaven united under one common fatherhood and bearing, as a clan does, the name of its ancestor. Robertson dismisses the alternative in a phrase as most unlikely, taking the word of descent from a common ancestor. Clarke fastens on the singular: Paul does not say families, as though each order formed its own household, but family, because they are all one and of one, deriving their being and their name from God as children take the name of the head of their house. A note carried in Calvin's column, credited to Chandler, sets this against the local cult: Diana was the common goddess of the Asiatic cities, her temple built by their common contributions, and she presided over that federation as its mother and patroness — and the Ephesians are told they now belong to a nobler family.

Clarke calls the petition that follows one of the most grand and sublime in the whole oracles of God, says no paraphrase can do it justice, and suspects few commentators have entered into its spirit, deterred by its unparalleled sublimity. On the measure of the gift he offers a homely comparison: in almsgiving the maxim is that each should give according to his ability, and it would disgrace a king to give no more than a tradesman — God acts up to the dignity of his infinite perfections. Ellicott traces the movement of the prayer from the Father, as the source of all being, to the Spirit as the giver of life, and distinguishes it from the earlier petition in the letter. That one asked for illumination and named only the eyes of the heart; this asks for strength and takes in the inner man entire, with all his faculties. The difference matters, he says, because light is a gift from outside while strength comes from an indwelling power. Calvin adds that no believer ever advances so far as to need no further growth, the highest perfection of the godly in this life being an earnest desire to make progress. Cyril of Jerusalem quotes the verse in passing, among his proofs that the Spirit of the Father is the Comforter under another name.
17:
Gill is careful to say what the indwelling is not. It is not the omnipresence of Christ as God, nor his dwelling in the human nature, nor merely a presence by his Spirit, but a personal indwelling of his own — as a king in his palace, to rule and protect; as a master in his household, to provide; as their life, to quicken them. Calvin uses the clause to bind two gifts together. It is a mistake to imagine that the Spirit can be had without Christ, and equally foolish to dream that we can receive Christ without the Spirit; we partake of the Spirit in proportion to the intercourse we keep with Christ, since the Spirit rests nowhere but on him, and Christ cannot be separated from his Spirit without being reckoned dead. That the heart is named he takes as deliberate: it is not enough if the knowledge of Christ dwells on the tongue or flutters in the brain. Wesley glosses the verb as abiding constantly and sensibly. Robertson notes that the word means to make one's home, to be at home, and cannot resist the obvious remark — this is the ideal, but a deal of fixing would have to be done in our hearts before Christ could be at home in them.

Clarke reads the whole prayer as a dedication. The church is a temple built to be a habitation of God through the Spirit, and Paul, having seen the Ephesian church completely formed in every outward thing, does what Solomon did at Jerusalem and prays that God would come down and dwell in it. He then runs the figure back through the whole history: man was formed at the beginning to be God's temple and was inhabited while he remained pure; when the temple was defiled God left it; Christ the repairer of the breach comes to purify it and make it fit again. The warning follows at once — a heart that is not God's house must be a hold of every foul and unclean spirit, since Satan and his angels will fill what God does not. Ellicott insists that the indwelling of Christ is not a consequence of the gift of the Spirit but identical with it, the Spirit's office being to work out in us the likeness of Christ; faith is simply the condition, the opening of the door. Calvin sharpens the same point against a common confusion: most people treat believing in Christ and fellowship with Christ as one thing, whereas the fellowship follows the faith — for faith is not a distant view of Christ but a warm embrace of him.

"Rooted and grounded" mixes a metaphor, and nobody minds. Barnes takes the first from a tree whose roots strike deep and far, the second from architecture, where a firm foundation is laid, and wants the love of Christ as fixed in the heart as a building on solid rock. Robertson observes that Paul is piling up metaphors — dwelling, rooted, grounded — and adds a structural point: the two participles are nominative and belong with what follows, so that the next verse should really begin with them. Ellicott calls the mixture so natural as to have passed into common usage, and distinguishes the two ideas, the one of striking deeper and spreading wider into the soil, the other of the basis on which we finally rest. He then enters a caution that Calvin enters independently. Love is not itself the root or the foundation, for that is Christ; it is the condition under which growth takes place. Calvin puts it as a warning against a false inference: it is idle to conclude from these words that love is the foundation of our salvation, since Paul is not asking here on what our salvation rests, but with what firmness and constancy we ought to continue in loving.
18:
Breadth, length, depth and height — of what? Ellicott answers that Paul has of set purpose omitted the noun, leaving the phrase in absolute generality, so that no answer can be perfectly satisfactory; if anything is to be supplied it should be the mystery itself, with its predestination, redemption, and calling of Jew and Gentile. The others each supply something. Barnes reports Locke's guess at the calling of the Gentiles and Chandler's that the words allude to the temple of Diana at Ephesus, one of the wonders of the world and a standing object of local pride; but he sees no clear evidence for it, and takes the words simply as a full heart's way of saying how great that love is. Clarke knows the Diana theory, gives its dimensions and its hundred and twenty-seven pillars, and rejects it — Paul had a nobler model at hand in the temple at Jerusalem, built to be a habitation of God. Calvin is briskest of all. Augustine, delighted with his own acuteness, found an allusion to the figure of the cross and assigned love, hope, patience and humility to the four dimensions; Ambrose found a sphere; neither, says Calvin, has anything to do with Paul's meaning, which is simply the love of Christ. Wesley measures that love out in four clauses.

Knowing what passes knowledge is felt by all of them as a paradox. Clarke offers two ways out: the verb may mean to approve or publicly acknowledge, and we can acknowledge what we cannot comprehend; but he thinks it likelier that the noun means science in general, and particularly the science the rabbis boasted of as the key of knowledge and the Greeks exulted in while reckoning all other nations barbarians — against all of which the love of Christ is set. Ellicott refuses the easier solution. There is no trace here of an opposition in kind between spiritual knowing and mere head-knowledge; rather the tense expresses cognition in a particular case, so that the prayer is to know from time to time, as each occasion offers, what in its entirety must always pass discovery, going on from knowledge to knowledge and still finding new depths to be fathomed. Gill grants that the saints' knowledge, though experimental and appropriating and exceeding all other knowledge, remains imperfect. Robertson lets the difficulty stand and admires the nerve of it: all the same, Paul dares to scale this peak.

On the last clause Clarke and Calvin pull in opposite directions. Clarke calls it the greatest saying in the prayer and refuses all softening: most people, in quoting the words, try to correct the apostle by inserting "communicable," which he thinks as idle as it is impertinent, since Paul means what he says. To be filled with all the fulness of God is to have the whole soul filled with meekness, goodness, love, justice, holiness, mercy and truth — and since what God fills neither sin nor Satan can fill, it implies a soul emptied of sin. Calvin guards the other flank, calling it a foolish and wicked dream to take the fulness for the full Godhead, as though men were raised to an equality with God; the phrase means having in Christ everything necessary to be made perfect in God. Ellicott's grammatical correction quietly reconciles them: the preposition is not "with" but "up to," so that the clause describes conformation to the image of him in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Wesley itemises it as light, love, wisdom, holiness, power and glory, a perfection far beyond a bare freedom from sin.
20:
The doxology's central clause defeats translation, and all three of the closest readers say so. Robertson notes that the adverb is a rare double compound suiting Paul's effort to pile Pelion on Ossa; the verb for asking is middle, we ask for ourselves, and the highest aspiration a man can form is still not beyond God's power to bestow. Wesley traces a gradation through the whole: when God has given us exceeding and abundant blessings we may still ask for more, and he is able; we may think of more than we have asked, and he is able for that too; and then above all this. Clarke pushes the same ladder further. We can ask every good promised in the word; we can imagine blessings beyond anything we have read of or seen, goods to which we cannot even give a name, going past the limits of all human description — and after all this God is able to do more. He then adds the point that makes the praise usable: God's ability here is so necessarily bound to his willingness that the one implies the other, since it would be no comfort to tell the church he had the power if there were no assurance that he will use it.

Gill uses the occasion to define the divine power carefully, and is willing to name its limits. It reaches to everything God wills, to more than he has willed, and to things impossible with men; yet there are things God cannot do — whatever is contrary to his nature, inconsistent with his decrees, or implies a contradiction — since to do them would be to deny himself. Calvin insists the word is not power viewed apart from its exercise but power actually exerted and felt: whatever God can do he will unquestionably do, if he has promised it, and the appeal to the power that works in us points to what the Ephesians had already experienced in their own conversion. From that he draws a striking permission — the phrase bids us entertain no fear that faith of the proper kind might run to excess, since whatever expectations we form of divine blessing, the infinite goodness of God will exceed all our wishes and all our thoughts. Gill also fixes the place where the glory is rendered: the church, because there alone are the mysteries of grace known and men know how to glorify God aright. Henry states the practical rule the whole passage teaches: it is proper always to end our prayers with praises.

Ellicott hears the epistle's governing idea in the parallel clauses: what is in the church is in Christ Jesus, the visible unity representing the invisible unity it depends on. The closing formula he renders literally — to all the generations of the age of the ages — and takes it as picturing each generation adding its own thanksgiving to a chorus of praise that fills eternity. Barnes agrees the phrase resists translation, calling it one of the apostle's self-invented expressions and citing Blackwall that no version conveys it. In the remarks he appends to the chapter he turns its doctrine against every attempt to confine the gospel to a favoured class — by caste sustained from age to age by priesthood and law, by ancestry, by wealth, or by complexion, where men have supposed one class the favourite of heaven for having a skin not coloured like others and doomed the rest to servitude. Clarke closes with an estimate of the chapter itself. For the importance of its matter and the sublimity of its conceptions he thinks no portion of the New Testament equal to it; the apostle was shut up in prison, but the word of the Lord was not bound, and his own nervous language seems to bend and tremble under the weight of the ideas it carries.
